parts.title: A week with my uncle in Morocco
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last summer, I stayed for a week with my uncle Karim, who lives in a small town on the edge of the Sahara. I was very excited, because I had only seen the desert in films.

On the first morning, my uncle woke me at five. "We must walk before the sun gets high," he said. It was already warm, but the sand was cool under my feet. We climbed a big dune, and from the top I could see nothing but gold in every direction. I felt very small.

My uncle works as a guide, and he taught me a lot. He showed me how to wrap a long scarf around my head to keep out the sun and the sand. He also told me never to go anywhere without at least two litres of water, even for a short walk.

The nights were the best part. After dinner, we lay on a blanket and counted the shooting stars. I had never seen so many. When I left, my uncle gave me a small bag of sand from the dune. It is on my desk now, and every time I look at it, I want to go back.

questions.prompt: Why was the writer excited about the visit?
options: He had only seen deserts in films
He wanted to learn to speak Arabic
He had never stayed with his uncle
questions.explanation: He had only seen the desert in films.

questions.prompt: Why did they walk early in the morning?
options: The sun was not high yet
His uncle had to go to work
The sand was too cold later
questions.explanation: They must walk before the sun gets high.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel on top of the dune?
options: Very small in the big landscape
questions.explanation: From the top he could see gold in every direction and felt very small.

options: Leave some in a bottle at home

questions.explanation: He told him never to go anywhere without at least two litres of water.

questions.prompt: What did the writer do in the evenings?
options: He studied maps with his uncle
He helped to cook dinner for guests
He watched shooting stars at night
questions.explanation: After dinner they lay on a blanket and counted shooting stars.

parts.title: The camel, the ship of the desert
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
People often call the camel the ship of the desert, and there is a good reason for this. [1] It can walk for many days across hot sand and carry a heavy load.

A camel has a hump on its back. Many people think the hump is full of water, but this is not true. [2] When there is no food, the camel slowly uses the fat, and the hump gets smaller.

Camels also have very long eyelashes. [3] Their wide, flat feet help them too, because they do not sink into the soft sand.

Although camels can live without water for a long time, they drink a lot when they find it. [4] After that, they can walk again for a week or more.

For thousands of years, people have used camels for travel and trade. [5] Today, they are still important in many places, and some tourists enjoy riding them.
sentences: It stores fat, which gives the animal energy when it is hungry.
They protect the eyes from the wind and the blowing sand.
The animal is perfectly made for a life in very dry places.
A thirsty camel can drink over a hundred litres in only a few minutes.
Camels were first brought to Australia about two hundred years ago.
Without them, long journeys across the desert would have been almost impossible.

gaps.explanation: The sentence about being perfectly made for dry places follows the name "ship of the desert" and leads to "it can walk for many days".
The hump is not full of water, but it stores fat, which the next sentence says the camel uses.
The eyelashes protect the eyes from the wind and sand, and the next sentence adds the feet.
The camel drinks a hundred litres in minutes, and "after that" it can walk for a week.
Journeys across the desert would have been almost impossible without them, which links to "used camels for travel".

parts.title: Staying cool in hot weather
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: When the weather is very hot, it is important to look after yourself. First of all, you should drink plenty of water, even [1] you do not feel thirsty. It is also a good idea to wear light clothes and a hat to keep the sun [2] your head. Many people go out early in the morning or late in the evening, when it is much [3] hot. During the middle of the day, it is better to stay [4] a cool room or in the shade. Children and old people need extra care, because they can get ill [5] quickly. If you feel dizzy, sit down and rest [6] a few minutes.

gaps.explanation: "Even if you do not feel thirsty" is a fixed phrase.
Keep the sun off your head.
Much less hot: comparison of a smaller degree.
They can get ill more quickly.

parts.title: A talk about the Sahara
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: saskia
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Today, I will tell you about the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world. It is about as big as the United States, and it covers eleven countries in Africa. Many people think that the Sahara is all sand, but in fact, only about one fifth of it is covered by sand dunes. The rest is made up of rocks, mountains and dry valleys. In the daytime, the temperature can reach fifty degrees, but at night it can fall to almost zero. Very little rain falls there, often less than two centimetres in a year. Even so, some animals live in the desert, such as the fennec fox, a small animal with enormous ears that help it to stay cool. People also live there, and the best known group are the Tuareg, who wear blue clothes and travel across the sand with their camels.

gaps.explanation: It covers eleven countries in Africa.

gaps.prompt: Only one ___ of the desert is sand
gaps.explanation: Only about one fifth of it is covered by sand dunes.
The temperature can reach fifty degrees.

gaps.prompt: The fennec fox has very big ___
gaps.explanation: A small animal with enormous ears.

gaps.prompt: A well-known group of people are the ___
gaps.explanation: The best known group are the Tuareg.

parts.title: An interview with a desert photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Adriana, you take pictures of deserts all over the world. When did you start?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: My father gave me a camera for my twelfth birthday, and I took it everywhere. A year later, we visited Arizona, and I fell in love with the desert.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is so special about deserts for you?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: The light. In the morning and the evening, the sand turns orange and red, and the shadows are long. Every ten minutes, the picture is different.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the hardest part of your work?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Carrying the equipment. My bag weighs twenty kilos, and I often walk for hours in the heat. Sand also gets inside the camera, so I have to clean it every night.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is there a place that you would like to visit?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Yes, the Atacama in Chile. It is the driest place on Earth, and some years, no rain falls at all. People say the night sky there is the clearest in the world.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young photographer?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Be patient. I once waited all day for the perfect picture of a lizard, and it only appeared at sunset. But it was worth it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And what are you working on now?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: A book about the people of the desert. I want to show that, even in a harsh place, people have a rich and happy life.
